hints: Think about what two quantities a moving object must have for its motion to be hard to stop - how heavy it is and how fast it is moving.
walkthrough:
**What momentum means**
Think of momentum as the quantity of motion. A heavy slow lorry and a light fast bullet can both be hard to stop. So you need both mass $m$ and velocity $v$ together.

**Exact definition**
Momentum is defined by $$p = m \times v$$ It is a vector, so it has direction the same as the velocity, with SI unit $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$.
Final answer: the product of mass and velocity

hints: Look at Fig. 2.2 for block Y - when does its momentum first start to change from zero, and when does it stop changing and become flat again?
walkthrough:
**When is there a force on Y?**
Block Y is stationary with zero momentum until X touches it. While they touch, X pushes Y so the momentum of Y changes. Once they separate, there is no more push, so the momentum of Y stays constant.

**Read the start and end from the graph**
In Fig. 2.2 the graph leaves zero at $t = 60\text{ ms}$ and stops rising at $t = 100\text{ ms}$. So contact lasts $$\Delta t = 100 - 60 = 40\text{ ms}$$

hints: For fixed mass, acceleration is proportional to the gradient of a momentum–time graph.
walkthrough: During the straight sloping section, momentum changes at a constant rate, so the acceleration has constant magnitude.
During the horizontal section, momentum and velocity are constant, so acceleration is zero.

hints: Force is the rate of change of momentum, so focus on the sloping section where Y gains momentum - what is the total change in momentum and over what time?
Convert the contact time to seconds and divide the momentum change by this time to get force in newtons.
walkthrough:
**Choose the governing law**
Force on Y equals its rate of gain of momentum: $$F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$$ This is the gradient of the sloping part of Fig. 2.2.

**Find change in momentum and time**
Momentum of Y rises from $0$ to $0.50\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$, so $\Delta p = 0.50\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$. Contact time from (b)(i) is $$\Delta t = 40\text{ ms} = 40 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}$$

**Calculate the force**
$$F = \frac{0.50}{40 \times 10^{-3}} = 12.5\text{ N} \approx 13\text{ N}$$ This is the magnitude of the force exerted by X on Y during contact.

hints: Before contact X feels no force, so what should its momentum graph look like from $t = 0$ to $t = 60\text{ ms}$ given it starts at $0.40\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$?
Total momentum must stay at $0.40\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ because there are no external forces - if Y ends at $0.50\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$, what must the final momentum of X be?
During contact X loses momentum at the same rate Y gains it, so how should the slope of X between $60\text{ ms}$ and $100\text{ ms}$ compare to the slope of Y?
walkthrough:
**Before collision - constant momentum**
From $t = 0$ to $60\text{ ms}$ there is no contact and no friction, so X keeps its initial momentum. Draw a horizontal line from $(0, 0.40)$ to $(60, 0.40)$ in units $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$ and $\text{ms}$.

**Use conservation to find the end point**
Total momentum is conserved at $0.40\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$. At the end: $$p_X + p_Y = 0.40$$ With $p_Y = 0.50\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$, $$p_X = 0.40 - 0.50 = -0.10\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$$ The negative sign means X rebounds backwards. So the graph must finish at $-0.10$.

**During and after collision**
During contact, $60$ to $100\text{ ms}$, X loses momentum steadily while Y gains it, so draw a straight line from $(60, 0.40)$ down to $(100, -0.10)$. After $100\text{ ms}$ the blocks are separate, so draw a horizontal line from $(100, -0.10)$ to $(160, -0.10)$.

Final answer: Horizontal line at $0.40\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ from $t=0$ to $60\text{ ms}$, straight line down to $-0.10\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ at $t=100\text{ ms}$, then horizontal at $-0.10\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ to $160\text{ ms}$.
